This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

lem-bounded-lipschitz-metric-characteriz.claim: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(S,d)$ be a Polish space, and let $\mu_n,\mu$ be Borel probability measures on $S$. Define

citations.quote: For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.
Assume AC. A family $\mathcal A$ of Borel probabilities on a Polish space S is tight if and only if it is relatively sequentially compact for weak convergence.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

derivations.claim:
Nonnegativity, symmetry and the triangle inequality for $ eta_{BL}$ follow by applying these properties to the difference of the two test integrals and then taking the supremum. If $ eta_{BL}(
u,ho)=0$, fix a nonempty closed $F$ and put $g_m=(1-md(\cdot,F))_+$. The function $g_m/m$ is an admissible test, so $\int g_m\,d
u=\int g_m\,dho$. By [F4], these integrals decrease to $
u(F)$ and $ho(F)$, respectively. The two probabilities therefore agree on every closed set, including the empty set. Closed sets form a pi-system generating the Borel sigma-algebra, and both total masses are one, so [F6] gives $
u=ho$. Thus $ eta_{BL}$ is a metric; this argument uses no choice.

Assume $\beta_{BL}(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$, and fix a nonempty closed set $F\subseteq S$. For every integer $m\ge1$, the function $g_m(x)=(1-md(x,F))_+$ satisfies $0\le g_m\le1$ and $\operatorname{Lip}_d(g_m)\le m$. Hence $g_m/m$ is admissible in the definition of $\beta_{BL}$, so $\int g_m\,d\mu_n\to\int g_m\,d\mu$. Since $1_F\le g_m$, it follows that $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\int g_m\,d\mu$ for every $m$.

Now assume $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$, and put $\mathcal A=\{\mu\}\cup\{\mu_n:n\ge1\}$. Any sequence chosen from $\mathcal A$ either has a member repeated infinitely often, yielding a constant convergent subsequence, or has a subsequence of the form $(\mu_{n_j})$ with $n_j\to\infty$, which converges weakly to $\mu$. Therefore $\mathcal A$ is relatively sequentially compact for weak convergence.

The functions $g_m$ decrease pointwise to $1_F$ and are bounded by the integrable constant function $1$ under the probability $\mu$. By [F4], $\int g_m\,d\mu\to\mu(F)$, so the closed-set bound holds; it is trivial for $F=\varnothing$. The Portmanteau theorem [F2] gives weak convergence in the sense of [F1].

By [F5], $S$ is Polish; therefore [F3] applies under [A1] and $\mathcal A$ is tight. Thus for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq S$ such that $\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal A}\nu(K^c)<\varepsilon$.

Fix $\eta>0$. Compactness gives a finite $\eta/8$-net $x_1,\dots,x_q$ of $K$. Quantize each value $g(x_i)\in[-1,1]$ into finitely many bins of width at most $\eta/2$. There are finitely many resulting value patterns for the bounded 1-Lipschitz test class; choose one representative $h_r$ from each nonempty pattern. If $g$ and $h_r$ share a pattern, then for $x\in K$ a net point $x_i$ gives $|g(x)-h_r(x)|\le2d(x,x_i)+|g(x_i)-h_r(x_i)|<\eta$.

For any admissible $g$, choose the representative $h_r$ from its pattern. The integral difference is bounded by $\left|\int g\,d\mu_n-\int g\,d\mu\right|\le\max_r\left|\int h_r\,d\mu_n-\int h_r\,d\mu\right|+2\eta+2\mu_n(K^c)+2\mu(K^c).$ The maximum tends to zero by [F1], because there are finitely many bounded continuous representatives, and the last two terms are at most $4\varepsilon$ by step 2.2. Taking the supremum over $g$, then the limit superior in $n$, gives $\limsup_n\beta_{BL}(\mu_n,\mu)\le2\eta+4\varepsilon$. Letting $\eta,\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves the reverse implication.

citations.quote:
Use the wavelet coefficient levels $(l,k)$ and multiplicities $|K_l|=2^l$ from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. Let $w=(w_l)$ be nondecreasing with $w_l\ge1$. Define
$$M(w)=\left\{x=(x_{lk}):\|x\|_{M(w)}:=\sup_l\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}<\infty\right\}$$
and its closed little-o subspace
$$M_0(w)=\left\{x\in M(w):\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}\longrightarrow0\text{ as }l\to\infty\right\},$$
with the same norm. Call $w$ admissible when $w_l/\sqrt l\to\infty$. The finite coarsest level is included in the norm and does not affect this limit. Elements are coefficient sequences; in particular, they need not be $L^2$ functions. [[lem-m0w-separable-and-projection-tails]] proves that $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space, that $L^2$ coefficient sequences embed in it, and that finite-level projections converge in its norm.

For every weight sequence in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space. If $P_J$ retains exactly the coefficients at levels $l\le J$, then $\|P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\le\|x\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\to0$ for each $x\in M_0(w)$. Every square-summable coefficient sequence belongs to $M_0(w)$.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a compactly supported wavelet basis of [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The Haar basis with its finite scaling coordinate, as specified in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], is also allowed. Assume each level-$l$ wavelet for $l\ge l_0$ has zero integral, uniformly bounded overlap, support length at most $C_0 2^{-l}$, and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_1\le C_0 2^{-l/2}$. Let $M_0(w)$ be as in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], and suppose
$$S_w:=\sum_{l\ge l_0}w_l2^{-l/2}<\infty.$$
For $x\in M_0(w)$ define
$$Jx(t):=\sum_{l,k}x_{lk}\langle 1_{[0,t]},\psi_{lk}\rangle_{L^2},\qquad 0\le t\le1.$$
Then this series converges absolutely and uniformly in $t$, $Jx\in C([0,1])$, and $\|Jx-Jy\|_\infty\le C S_w\|x-y\|_{M(w)}$ after adding the finite coarsest-level constant to $C S_w$. If $x$ is the coefficient sequence of $f\in L^2$, then $Jx(t)=\int_0^t f(u)\,du$.

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

Write $\mathbb Q$ for the canonical image of the rationals in $\mathbb R$ under the embedding of [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]].

Let $y\mapsto\Pi_y$ be a probability kernel on $\mathbb R$. For $u\in(0,1)$ put
$$F_y(t)=\Pi_y((-\infty,t]),\qquad q_u(y)=\inf\{r\in\mathbb Q:F_y(r)\ge u\}.$$The infimum is taken in $\mathbb R$; [[thm-infimum-property]] supplies it once the defining set is shown nonempty and bounded below. Then $q_u:\mathsf Y\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, and$$\Pi_y((-\infty,q_u(y)))\le u\le\Pi_y((-\infty,q_u(y)]).$$

Let $Q_n(y,\cdot)$ be data-indexed probability kernels on $\mathbb R$, let $Q$ be a fixed law with continuous CDF $F$, and suppose $\beta_{BL}(Q_n(y,\cdot),Q)\to0$ in probability. Fix $0<u<1$ and let $q=q_u(Q):=\inf\{r\in\mathbb Q:Q((-∞,r])\ge u\}$, using the canonical rational embedding. Assume $F$ is strictly increasing on some open interval containing $q$. Define $q_u(Q_n(y,\cdot))$ by the same convention. Then $q_u(Q_n)\to q$ in probability. The local strict-increase hypothesis permits CDFs, such as norms of nonnegative random elements, that are constant on part of $\mathbb R$.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be measurable spaces and let $y\mapsto\Pi_y$ be a supplied posterior probability kernel. For $\alpha\in[0,1]$, a set-valued rule $C$ is **graph-measurable** when
$$\{(y,\theta)\in\mathsf Y\times\Theta:\theta\in C(y)\}\in\mathcal Y\otimes\mathcal T.$$
It is a **posterior credible set at level $1-\alpha$** when it is graph-measurable and
$$\Pi_y(C(y))\ge 1-\alpha\qquad\text{for every }y\text{ in its declared data domain}.$$
The posterior-mass function is measurable by integration of the indicator of the membership graph against the kernel. If a density is available relative to a specified dominating measure, a highest-posterior-density region selects parameter values with largest density; such regions need not be intervals and may be disconnected or nonunique.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

Assume AC. Let $P_0$ have a density $f_0$ on $[0,1]$ with $\|f_0\|_\infty\le B<\infty$. Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be an orthonormal, compactly supported wavelet basis with $2^l$ coefficients at level $l\ge1$, uniformly bounded overlap, and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_\infty\le C_0 2^{l/2}$. Suppose for some $\gamma>1/2$,
$$\max_k|\langle f_0,\psi_{lk}\rangle|\le C_f2^{-l(\gamma+1/2)}.$$
Let $w_l\ge1$ be nondecreasing and admissible in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], and choose either cutoff regime
$$2^{L_n}\asymp n^{1/(2\gamma+1)}\quad\text{or}\quad 2^{L_n}\asymp(n/\log n)^{1/(2\gamma+1)}.$$
For IID $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P_0$, define the finite wavelet projection $P_n(L_n)$ by coefficients $\langle P_n(L_n),\psi_{lk}\rangle=P_n\psi_{lk}:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_{lk}(X_i)$ for $l\le L_n$ and zero for $l>L_n$, with the coarsest scaling coordinates projected as well. Let $G_{P_0}$ be a Borel centered Gaussian law on $M_0(w)$ whose coefficient covariance is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(G_{lk},G_{l'k'})=P_0[(\psi_{lk}-P_0\psi_{lk})(\psi_{l'k'}-P_0\psi_{l'k'})].$$
Then
$$\sqrt n\{P_n(L_n)-f_0\}\Rightarrow G_{P_0}\quad\text{in }M_0(w).$$

$X_n\to X$ in probability if and only if every subsequence of $(X_n)$ has a
further subsequence converging almost surely to $X$.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves that this coefficient map is a continuous embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The product-prior theorem below uses the wavelet case.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

derivations.claim:
The posterior draw $f$ and center $T_n$ are $L^2$-valued, so [F2] embeds $\sqrt n(f-T_n)$ in $M_0(w)$; [F1] supplies its norm. For an $L$-Lipschitz map $T$ between metric spaces and any admissible bounded 1-Lipschitz test $h$ on its target, $h\circ T/\max(1,L)$ is an admissible test on its domain. Therefore
$$\beta_{BL}(T_\#\nu,T_\#\rho)\le\max(1,L)\beta_{BL}(\nu,\rho).$$
By [F3], $J$ is linear and Lipschitz with a finite constant $L_J$. The bound applied pointwise to the data-indexed laws in [A1] gives $\beta_{BL}(J_\#Q_n,J_\#G_{P_0})\to0$ in probability. Moreover, if $\ell:C([0,1])\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and linear, then $\ell\circ J$ is continuous and linear on $M_0(w)$. The centered Gaussian premise on $G_{P_0}$ says exactly that this scalar pushforward is centered normal, allowing zero variance. Thus $J_\#G_{P_0}$ is a centered Gaussian Borel law. In particular, for any finite $t_1,\ldots,t_m$ and real $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, the functional $x\mapsto\sum_i a_iJx(t_i)$ is continuous and linear, so the evaluation vector $(JG_{P_0}(t_i))_{i=1}^m$ is jointly centered Gaussian. This uses only the scalar Gaussian pushforward meaning of the premise, without characteristic-function uniqueness or a Gaussian existence theorem. To identify its covariance, let $p_J1_{[0,s]}$ be the finite wavelet projection of the indicator. The finite Gaussian coefficient covariance gives
$$\operatorname{Cov}(J(P_JG_{P_0})(s),J(P_JG_{P_0})(t))=P_0[(p_J1_{[0,s]}-P_0p_J1_{[0,s]})(p_J1_{[0,t]}-P_0p_J1_{[0,t]})].$$
By [F11], $p_J1_{[0,s]}\to1_{[0,s]}$ in Lebesgue $L^2$; since $f_0\le B$, this is also convergence in $L^2(P_0)$. The variance of a difference of two finite projected Gaussian evaluations is the $P_0$-variance of the corresponding difference of projected indicators, so it tends to zero; hence those evaluations are Cauchy in $L^2$. They also converge almost surely to $JG_{P_0}(s)$ because $P_JG_{P_0}\to G_{P_0}$ in $M_0(w)$ and $J$ is continuous. The almost-sure and in-probability limits coincide: for any $\varepsilon>0$, the probability that they differ by more than $\varepsilon$ is bounded by the two probabilities that each sequence differs from its limit by more than $\varepsilon/2$, both tending to zero. If $U_J,V_J$ are the projected evaluations and $U,V$ their $L^2$ limits, [F12] gives
$$|\mathbb E[U_JV_J]-\mathbb E[UV]|\le\|U_J-U\|_2\|V_J\|_2+\|U\|_2\|V_J-V\|_2\longrightarrow0;$$
the norms $\|V_J\|_2$ are bounded because $V_J\to V$ in $L^2$, and the means converge to zero as well. Thus the finite covariance passes to the limit. The resulting covariance is $P_0[(1_{[0,s]}-F_0(s))(1_{[0,t]}-F_0(t))]=F_0(s\wedge t)-F_0(s)F_0(t)$, the defining covariance of the $P_0$-Brownian bridge.

The norm maps $x\mapsto\|x\|_{M(w)}$ and $F\mapsto\|F\|_\infty$ are 1-Lipschitz by the reverse triangle inequality. Applying the pushforward bound of step 1.1 first to the $M(w)$ norm and then to the supremum norm after $J$ gives bounded-Lipschitz convergence in probability of both posterior norm laws to their corresponding limit norm laws. Their CDFs satisfy [A3], so [F6] gives $R_n^M\to q_M$ and $R_n^C\to q_C$ in probability. For the projected empirical center $T_n=P_n(L_n)$, [F9] verifies [A2] under the smoothness and cutoff assumptions in [F9].

The posterior pushforward under either norm is a probability kernel on $[0,\infty)$. By [F5], the two lower quantiles are measurable and their posterior CDFs at those radii are at least $1-\alpha$. Since the centers and norms are measurable, the membership graphs of $C_n^M$ and $C_n^C$ are measurable. Thus both sets are credible by [F7].

By [A2] and [F4], $\sqrt n(T_n-f_0)\Rightarrow G_{P_0}$ and its primitive converges weakly to $B_{P_0}$. The frequentist error uses the negative center difference, but $\|f_0-T_n\|_{M(w)}=\|T_n-f_0\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|J(f_0-T_n)\|_\infty=\|J(T_n-f_0)\|_\infty$ because $J$ is linear. Thus each scaled frequentist error norm converges to the corresponding limit norm in [A3]. On the event that the random radius is within $\varepsilon$ of its deterministic limit from step 1.2, coverage is bounded above and below by probabilities for the frequentist norm with fixed thresholds expanded or contracted by $\varepsilon$. [F8] gives convergence of those fixed-threshold probabilities because [A3] makes their boundary probabilities zero. Sending $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and using the CDF value $1-\alpha$ at its quantile from [A3] yields $1-\alpha$ for both coverage probabilities. This comparison does not require independence between the data-dependent posterior radii and the frequentist center.
